title: Khamenei's Funeral: A Spectacle of Symbolism and Political Messaging
summary: The funeral of Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who died in a US-Israeli airstrike on February 28, has become a carefully orchestrated display of religious and political symbolism. Over a week of ceremonies, the Iranian government is leveraging imagery to promote unity among supporters and send a message to both domestic and international audiences. The official slogan, "We must rise" (and its Arabic equivalent "Rise for God"), is drawn from a Quranic verse calling Muslims to stand for a divine cause. This slogan appears on banners and images carried by mourners. A defining image of the funeral is an illustration of Khamenei's clenched fist on a red and black background. The fist is rooted in a text message attributed to his son and successor, Mojtaba Khamenei, who has not been seen publicly since becoming supreme leader in March due to security risks. The text said Mojtaba had "heard that the fist of [Khamenei's] healthy hand had been clenched." Red and black colors combine themes of grief, martyrdom, and a call for revenge. A giant red flag unfurled over the Grand Mosalla in Tehran reads "O avengers of Hussein" in Arabic, linking Khamenei's killing to the death of Prophet Muhammad's grandson at Karbala 1,300 years ago — an event that symbolizes resistance against illegitimate rule for many Shia Muslims. This frames retaliation against the US and Israel as a religious obligation, though it remains unclear how Iran will act. When General Qassem Soleimani was killed in 2020, Iran attacked US bases in Iraq without causing fatalities. The funeral procession route itself carries meaning: it travels from Qom (a center of clerical authority) to Najaf and Karbala in Iraq (holy Shia sites), and ends in Mashhad at the shrine of Imam Reza. This grand tour reinforces the ideological foundations of the Islamic Republic and its transnational Shia influence.
why_it_matters: The funeral shows how governments can use symbols, history, and religion to shape public emotion and justify future actions. Understanding this kind of political messaging helps young people recognize propaganda and think critically about why leaders emphasize certain narratives, especially during times of grief or conflict.

background_read: Ali Khamenei served as Iran’s Supreme Leader since 1989, holding the highest political and religious authority in the Islamic Republic under the concept of velayat-e faqih (guardianship of the jurist).
The flags and slogans draw on the Battle of Karbala (680 CE), where Hussein ibn Ali (Prophet Muhammad’s grandson) was killed—an event that is central to Shia identity and annual mourning ceremonies.
After the US killed General Qassem Soleimani in 2020, Iran retaliated with a missile attack on US bases in Iraq that caused no deaths, demonstrating a pattern of calibrated but symbolic responses.

Qom is Iran’s center of Shia scholarship; Najaf and Karbala in Iraq are among the holiest cities for Shia Islam; and Mashhad contains the shrine of Imam Reza, the eighth Shia imam, making the route a reinforcement of religious and transnational influence.
His son Mojtaba Khamenei was reported to have been chosen as his successor but has remained hidden due to security concerns, adding to the secrecy and symbolism around the leadership transition.

perspectives.description: For the regime’s supporters, the funeral turns a loss into a powerful rallying event, reinforcing resistance against foreign enemies and honoring a leader seen as a defender of Shia Islam. The symbolism connects contemporary politics to sacred history, strengthening national identity and a sense of purpose.

Critics argue that the state is exploiting grief to justify repression and possible military escalation, using religious imagery to stifle dissent. Some Iranians may feel the government is using the death to distract from domestic problems like economic hardship and political unrest.

Political funerals are often carefully staged events that blend ritual with propaganda. The choice of route and symbols reflects Iran’s strategy of projecting influence across the Shia world, leveraging historical narratives to assert legitimacy and maintain ideological cohesion.

The funeral’s call for revenge could increase tensions with the US and Israel, depending on whether Iran follows through with military action or chooses a more symbolic response, as it did after Soleimani’s killing. The hidden successor, Mojtaba, may emerge only when security allows, shaping how the leadership transition unfolds.
